title: The pool of nectar
hookLine: Guru Ram Das begins the pool and the town that will be named Amritsar, the pool of nectar

lines: GURU RAM DAS BEGINS TO DIG.
cards: Most towns grow up around something. A crossroads, a harbor, a mine, a railway station. Take away the thing in the middle and the town stops making sense.
Today, the beginning of a city millions visit every year, one of the most well-known in the world for Sikhs. It didn't grow up around a market or a fort.

Before it was a city, it was a patch of land with a small natural pond, surrounded by trees. Guru Amar Das, tradition says, asked Jetha, now his son-in-law, to find a place for a new center. And Guru Ram Das began to dig.

teach.b: The city is Amritsar. Amrit means nectar, the water of immortality, and sar means pool: the pool of nectar. At first the settlement was called Guru ka Chak, the Guru's village, and later Ramdaspur, after Guru Ram Das.
The name Amritsar came from the pool itself. Tradition says the Guru had the pond dug out and widened into a great tank, a sacred pool.
Sikhs came to help, carrying earth in baskets on their heads, the same work Jetha once did at the step-well. Here's the practical genius. The Guru didn't only build a place of worship.

He invited people to come and live there: traders and craftsmen of many kinds, tradition says, so the town would have its own markets and its own living. Worship and work, side by side; Kartarpur again, on a bigger scale.

teach.h: A STORY OF HEALING AT THE WATER.
teach.b: Sikhs tell a story about the pool, too. A young woman named Rajni, married off by her angry father to a man with leprosy, is said to have left her husband by the water while she went for food.
He saw a crow dip into the pool and come out white, bathed himself, and was healed. It's a story people tell, and the tree by that spot is still honored.
Guru Ram Das didn't live to see the pool finished; that would fall to his son.
But he gave the town its center, and the thing in the middle was a pool of still water.

how: Amritsar is the spiritual center of the Sikh world; pilgrims bathe in the sacred pool and walk around it, and many volunteer in its seva, cleaning the tank and serving in the langar.

o: the pool of nectar, and its city
a market town on a trade route

games.q: what's inside the name — tap the pairs.
p: an early name for the settlement
healed at the water, the story says

s: it began with a small pond that Guru Ram Das had dug into a sacred pool.
the Guru invited traders to settle there
worship and work, side by side, like Kartarpur.
Guru Ram Das finished the pool himself
it was completed under his son.

games.q: you're Guru Ram Das, starting a new center for the Sikhs. what do you put in the middle?
games.why: he dug out a pond into a sacred pool, and the town, later called Amritsar, grew up around it.

practice: Look at still water: a glass on the table, a bowl, a puddle, a sink you've filled. Watch the surface go still, the light on it, maybe your reflection, the tiny tremble when you breathe near it.
Let your mind settle the way the water does.

wordCard.voice: Amritsar. The pool of nectar; the sacred tank Guru Ram Das began, and the city that grew around it. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Amritsar, amrit, nectar, and sar, pool; the city named for its pool.

carryVoice: Your line: a town around a pool. Before the markets came, there was still water. That's fifty-five.

sources.ref: Sikh tradition (Bibi Rajni and the Dukh Bhanjani Beri)
